questions.q: State the three dimensions of the Human Development Index (HDI) and the specific indicator used for each dimension in the current UNDP methodology.
questions.a: The three dimensions are: (1) Long and healthy life — indicator: Life expectancy at birth (years); (2) Knowledge — indicators: Mean years of schooling (for adults aged 25+) and Expected years of schooling (for children of school-entry age); (3) Decent standard of living — indicator: Gross National Income (GNI) per capita at purchasing power parity (PPP $). A wrong answer that lists "GDP per capita" instead of "GNI per capita at PPP" reveals the student confuses domestic production with national income adjusted for cost of living, a common error in board exams where PPP adjustment is specifically tested.

questions.q: Why does the HDI use a geometric mean of the three dimension indices instead of an arithmetic mean (simple average)? Explain the economic reasoning.
questions.a: The geometric mean penalizes inequality across dimensions: if one dimension index is very low (e.g., 0.2), the geometric mean will be pulled down significantly, whereas an arithmetic mean would allow a high value in another dimension (e.g., 0.9) to compensate. This reflects the principle that health, education, and income are complementary — a country cannot "buy" good health with high income alone if the health system is absent. A wrong answer stating "geometric mean is easier to calculate" or "it gives more weight to income" reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the non-substitutability concept central to the capability approach.

questions.q: Country X has: Life expectancy at birth = 70 years, Mean years of schooling = 8 years, Expected years of schooling = 14 years, GNI per capita (PPP $) = 10,000. Using the standard goalposts (Life expectancy: 20–85; Mean years schooling: 0–15; Expected years schooling: 0–18; GNI per capita: 100–75,000), calculate the HDI for Country X. Show all steps.
questions.a:
Step 1: Calculate Health Index = (70 - 20) / (85 - 20) = 50/65 = 0.7692.
Step 2: Education Index = (Mean Years Index + Expected Years Index) / 2.
Mean Years Index = (8 - 0) / (15 - 0) = 8/15 = 0.5333.
Expected Years Index = (14 - 0) / (18 - 0) = 14/18 = 0.7778.
Education Index = (0.5333 + 0.7778) / 2 = 0.6555.
Step 3: Income Index = (ln(10000) - ln(100)) / (ln(75000) - ln(100)) = (9.2103 - 4.6052) / (11.2252 - 4.6052) = 4.6051 / 6.6200 = 0.6956.
Step 4: HDI = (0.7692 × 0.6555 × 0.6956)^(1/3) = (0.3505)^(1/3) = 0.705.
A wrong answer that uses arithmetic mean for the final step (0.7068) or forgets the natural log for income index reveals the student has memorized formulas but not the reasoning: income has diminishing returns, so log transformation is essential.

questions.q: Compare two countries: Country A has HDI 0.85 (Health 0.90, Education 0.85, Income 0.80). Country B has HDI 0.85 (Health 0.70, Education 0.90, Income 0.95). Which country has more balanced development? Justify using the properties of the geometric mean.
questions.a: Country A has more balanced development. The geometric mean equals the arithmetic mean only when all components are equal; the greater the disparity, the lower the geometric mean relative to the arithmetic mean. Country A's indices (0.90, 0.85, 0.80) have a smaller spread (range 0.10) than Country B's (0.70, 0.90, 0.95, range 0.25). For the same HDI (0.85), Country B must have higher individual indices in two dimensions to compensate for the low health index, proving its development is skewed. A wrong answer saying "both are equal because HDI is same" ignores the distributional information embedded in the geometric mean — a classic board exam trap in case-based questions.

questions.q: The Government of India is debating whether to allocate an additional ₹50,000 crore to building new AIIMS hospitals (health) or to a direct cash transfer scheme raising incomes of the poorest 20% (income). Using HDI logic, evaluate which investment would likely raise India's HDI more effectively, assuming current indices: Health 0.65, Education 0.60, Income 0.55.
questions.a: Investing in health (AIIMS) would raise HDI more. With current indices, the Health index (0.65) is the middle value, but the Income index (0.55) is the lowest. However, due to the log transformation in the income index, marginal increases in GNI per capita yield diminishing returns in the index. Conversely, life expectancy gains at India's current level (approx. 70 years) have linear returns in the health index. More importantly, better health improves education attendance and labor productivity — cross-dimensional synergies the geometric mean rewards. A wrong answer choosing cash transfers because "income is the lowest index" fails to account for diminishing returns in the income index formula and the complementarity between health and education.

questions.q: Construct a hypothetical example of a country that has "High Income" but "Low HDI". Specify plausible values for the four raw indicators (life expectancy, mean years schooling, expected years schooling, GNI per capita) that would produce this outcome. Explain why this disconnect occurs.
questions.a:
Country Z: Life expectancy = 55 years, Mean years schooling = 4 years, Expected years schooling = 9 years, GNI per capita = $40,000 (PPP).
Health Index = (55-20)/65 = 0.538. Education Index = ((4/15)+(9/18))/2 = (0.267+0.5)/2 = 0.383. Income Index = (ln(40000)-ln(100))/(ln(75000)-ln(100)) = (10.597-4.605)/6.620 = 0.905. HDI = (0.538×0.383×0.905)^(1/3) = (0.186)^(1/3) = 0.571 (Medium HDI). The disconnect occurs because the geometric mean prevents the high income index (0.905) from compensating for very low health and education indices. This mirrors resource-rich countries with poor social investment — a key HDI insight.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite statistical measure created by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) to assess a country's average ______ in three basic dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life (measured by life expectancy at birth), knowledge (measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling), and a decent standard of living (measured by Gross National Income per capita at purchasing power parity).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are comparing two Indian ______: Kerala and Bihar.
Fill in the blank: If we only compared per capita income (as in Node ______), we might miss that Kerala's advantage comes from decades of investing in public health and education.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate the HDI value for a country given the raw data for life expectancy, schooling years, and GNI per capita by applying the dimension index formulas and geometric mean.
